docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • This datasheet discusses the design, purpose, and rationale for the flow-sensing subsystem. This site also illustrates the contributions I made to this project.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
• This subsystem monitors the flow of liquid through a tube using a photoresistor. Originally, I wanted to use a hall-effect flow sensor, however since its output was digital, I was not able to use it and had to re-design the system to make use of a photoresistor.
  • To get more context as well as more information on all of our contributions take a look at the team report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
• I designed the flow-sensing board in its entirety and coordinated with teammates to ensure it would work with the other boards.

  • Below is list of pages for this site as well as a little context for what each entails.

  • To get a systems-level idea of how this subsystem will work, you can view the block diagram in the "Block Diagram" section of the datasheet.

  • To get context as to why certain major components were selected over others, you can view tables of my rationale in the "Component Selection" section of the datasheet.

  • To have a look at the materials used in the construction of this subsystem, you can view it in the "BOM" section of the datasheet.

  • To see how this subsystem is configured electrically, please view the "Schematic" section of the datasheet.

  • To understand the rationale for the selection of power components on the previous "Schematic" page, please view the Power Budget section of the datasheet.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The following block diagram describes the flow sensing subsystem I was responsible for. The board's purpose is to provide a status of whether or not water is flowing through the system. This device runs solely on +5v dc stepped down from +9v dc using a regulator. This board makes use of a photoresistor to detect whether or not water is flowing through a transparent tube. The photoresistor is connected to a circuit that drives an OpAmp chip where the output is eventually amplified and taken to the input on the PIC Curiosity Nano. My board is a "slave" board that communicates with the "master" board. This board exclusively outputs. The outputs consist of two wires that can be pulled high or low by the PIC totalling to 4 output states.

docs.text:
Here is informaiton regarding the rationale for selecting the components that will be put in my subsystem board.

Table 1: Flow Sensor component selection

Flow Sensor

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. 314150005 Flow Sensor $9.50/eachlink to product * Inexpensive* Accepts 5 Volts * Rated flow rate is desirable * Requires MOSFET to interact with PIC * Connectors require 1/2 inch piping * Option 2. * SLF3S-4000B Liquid Flow Sensor * $191.87/each * Link to product * Extremely Accurate * Communicates with I2C * Very expensive * Flow might be too small * Option 2. * SEN0216 Liquid Flow Sensor * $8.90/each * Link to product * Rated flow rate is desirable * Uses small 6mm ID piping * Might not be as accurate

Choice: Option 3: SEN0216 Liquid Flow Sensor

Rationale: This device uses a small ID tube which is better since we want to precisely control the amount we want to dispense. The amount of flow it is rated for should also be suitable.

Table 2: Flow Sensor Switching Mosfet component selection

Switching Mosfet

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Toshiba SSM3J36FS P-Channel Mosfet $0.27/eachlink to product * Voltage is desirable * Requires a negative supply voltage * Option 2. * Nexperia 2N7002NXAKR N-Channel Mosfet * $0.14/each * Link to product * N-Channel mosfet * Inexpensive * Heat sensitive * Option 3. Toshiba T2N7002AK N-Channel Mosfet * * $0.17/each * Link to product * Reputable manufacturer * Tried and true design * More expensive

Choice: Option 2: Nexperia 2N7002NXAKR N-Channel Mosfet

Rationale: This mosfet is best since it works within the limits of my proposed design as well as the price.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic was designed to detect liquid flowing through a transparent tube using a light sensor. When liquid flows through the tube, the light sensor will experience less light and increase its resistance. This will cause less voltage to get to the buffer and thus less voltage to reach the inverting amplifier. The PIC will notice the drop in voltage and understand that there is liquid flowing. It will then change its output state to the pre-determined state to tell the master unit that liquid is flowing.

Figure 1: Showing the current working schematic.
